tldr: We present CusADi2, a GPU library for robot kinematics and derivative evaluations. By parallelizing not only across batch instances but also within the internal computational graph of each instance, CusADi2 drastically cuts latency at batch sizes most common in online control (64 to 4096).
hero_caption: Speedup of CusADi2 across all 67 MuJoCo Menagerie robots (A) and the relationship between speedup and computational graph average width/maximum depth (B). CusADi2 achieves significantly lower latency than existing GPU and CPU baselines across batch sizes commonly used in online control (64 to 4096).
overview:
Online trajectory optimization for agile real-world robot control—such as sampling-based MPC or gradient-based methods—demands batch evaluations of dynamical system functions (forward kinematics, first-order Jacobians, and second-order Hessians) with extremely low latency.

However, existing GPU simulators and libraries (such as MuJoCo XLA and CusADi) were primarily designed for throughput-oriented workloads like reinforcement learning. In other words, they only use the GPU to parallelize across many trajectories, leaving the computation inside each trajectory strictly sequential. For small to medium batch sizes of a few hundred instances in online control, GPU cores remain idle, leading to long evaluation latencies.

To tackle this, the authors model computational functions as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and develop CusADi2, a level scheduling method that simultaneously assigns independent atomic operations (such as additions and trigonometric functions) within each instance to GPU cores. It also introduces windowing to handle saturated hardware cores, as well as operation sorting to prevent GPU warp divergence.

The authors benchmarked CusADi2 across all 67 robots in the MuJoCo Menagerie, including arms, multi-fingered hands, quadrupeds, and humanoids. CusADi2 outperformed all existing GPU backends at typical online control batch sizes of 64 to 4096, achieving speedups of up to tens of times at intermediate batch sizes. Furthermore, its low latency was demonstrated in a safety-filtered sampling-based MPC task on a Franka Panda arm.
contributions: Developed CusADi2, a GPU library that parallelizes internal computational graphs within each instance alongside parallelization across batch instances, achieving low latency required for online control.
Derived an optimal level schedule for the unsaturated regime and a windowed schedule that runs safely in the NP-hard saturated regime based on GPU core capacity.
Incorporated hardware-aware optimizations, including operation sorting to suppress GPU warp divergence and a staging optimization that reuses MPC timestep structures.

Demonstrated superior low latency compared to existing methods across all 67 robots in the MuJoCo Menagerie (with graphs up to ~430k nodes) and in a safety-critical MPC task at batch sizes of 64 to 4096.

sections.heading: Why is Low Latency Essential for GPU Robotics Computation?
sections.summary: While reinforcement learning prioritizes throughput over massive data, online trajectory optimization for real-time hardware execution critically depends on low latency for each batch. CusADi2 introduces intra-instance parallelization to solve this long-overlooked challenge.
sections.details:
Modern robotics relies heavily on algorithms like Model Predictive Control (MPC), which iteratively evaluate robot dynamics, forward kinematics, and their derivatives (Jacobians and Hessians). For instance, sampling-based MPC evaluates hundreds of trajectory rollouts simultaneously per control step, while gradient-based MPC evaluates Jacobians and Hessians along trajectories.

The critical bottleneck here is evaluation time—namely, latency. Latency directly dictates the achievable control frequency. However, existing GPU-based tools (such as MuJoCo XLA and CusADi) have been optimized primarily for reinforcement learning (RL). RL focuses on throughput—how many steps can be processed per unit time—often leaving low latency for individual batches behind.

Existing tools parallelize by assigning one trajectory (batch instance) to each GPU thread. With the smaller batch sizes typical of online control, GPU cores sit idle, and the wall-clock time required to complete a single computation does not decrease.

To resolve this, the paper proposes CusADi2. It analyzes the internal structure (computational graph) of the function and extracts parallelism *within* each instance to map onto the GPU. As a result, it evaluates forward kinematics for a batch of 256 instances in under 40 microseconds on typical robots.

sections.heading: The State of Batch Simulators, Latency Optimization, and Sparse Derivatives
sections.summary: Existing GPU tools fall into three areas: batch simulation, single-instance latency, and derivative sparsity. CusADi2 stands out by combining CasADi's fast, sparse symbolic differentiation with automatic intra-instance parallel scheduling.
sections.details:
Existing related work can be grouped into three main perspectives:

### Batch GPU Simulators
Recent GPU simulators (such as Isaac Gym, MuJoCo Warp, and JaxSim) are engineered for high throughput, running thousands to tens of thousands of independent environments simultaneously. However, they do not focus on delivering low latency at the scale of a few hundred batch instances needed for online deployment.

### Latency Reduction for Single Instances
Speeding up a single computation instance requires intra-instance parallelization. Frameworks relying on JAX or OpenXLA use heuristics tailored for large tensor operations in machine learning, struggling to effectively parallelize the fine-grained scalar operations common in robotics. Conversely, other frameworks require users to write hand-crafted parallel implementations for each instance, posing a major practical hurdle. CusADi2 fully automates this process.

### Handling Derivative Sparsity
Jacobians and Hessians for many robots exhibit sparse structures where most elements are zero. Yet many existing frameworks treat them as dense matrices, causing unnecessary computation. Some automatic differentiation tools support Jacobians but fail on Hessians, while symbolic differentiation tools often suffer from explosive compilation times or lack latency optimization. CusADi2 builds upon CasADi's fast, sparse symbolic differentiation pipeline and pairs it with GPU latency-reduction techniques.

sections.heading: Mapping Computational Graphs (DAGs) to GPU Cores in Minimal Time
sections.summary: Robot functions are formulated as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and framed as a scheduling problem to assign nodes to GPU units in minimal steps. Optimizing a single instance directly translates to lower overall batch latency.
sections.details:
To solve the problem of batch evaluation in minimal time, computational functions are represented as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) composed of atomic operations.

### A Minimal Computational Graph Example
Consider the function $g(x, y) = \sin(x) + \cos(y)$. This decomposes into three atomic operations: $\sin$, $\cos$, and addition $+$. Because $\sin(x)$ and $\cos(y)$ do not depend on each other, two GPU cores can compute them simultaneously. In other words, an evaluation that would take 3 sequential steps finishes in just 2 steps.

### From DAG to Schedule
For a general function $f$, we construct a DAG $\mathcal{D}_f$ with input vertices $\mathcal{I}$, work vertices $\mathcal{W}$, and output vertices $\mathcal{O}$. In practice, this DAG is extracted from CasADi's symbolic representation, allowing forward kinematics, Jacobians, and Hessians to be handled uniformly as DAGs.

Here, the GPU is abstracted as a collection of $N$ identical compute units. A tuple assigning an execution timestep $S_w \in \{1, \ldots, T\}$ to each computational vertex $w$ is defined as a schedule $S$. A valid schedule must satisfy the topological order constraint (parents must be computed before children) and the hardware saturation constraint (the number of concurrent operations must not exceed $N$).

### Schedule Width and Depth
The number of vertices executed concurrently at timestep $t$ is the schedule's width, and the final completion timestep is its depth. Depth is directly equivalent to execution latency. Therefore, the goal is a scheduling problem that minimizes depth under hardware constraints.

### From Instance to Batch
For a batch size $B$, if $B \times (\text{maximum width}) \leq N$, all instances in the batch can run in a single round. Hence, an optimal schedule for one instance directly yields the minimum batch latency. Even when capacity is exceeded, reducing single-instance depth remains the key to slashing overall batch latency.

sections.heading: Scheduling for Unsaturated and Saturated Regimes with GPU Optimizations
sections.summary: In the unsaturated regime with surplus cores, an optimal level schedule is used. In the saturated regime, a windowing heuristic partitions the DAG. GPU-specific vertex sorting suppresses warp divergence, and staging reuses repeated MPC step structures.
sections.details:
Although DAG scheduling is generally NP-hard, robotics computations often have ample GPU core capacity. Thus, the proposed method splits the problem into two regimes.

### IV-A Unsaturated Regime
When the available GPU cores exceed the graph's parallel width, a level schedule—where every vertex is scheduled immediately after its parents complete—is known to be strictly optimal (achieving minimal depth). Algorithm 1 constructs this optimal schedule in a single pass over topologically sorted nodes. On an RTX 4080, forward kinematics and Jacobians never saturated across all 67 Menagerie robots, and Hessians saturated for only 4 robots (6.0%).

### IV-B Saturated Regime
When the work vertices are so numerous that they exceed the core limit, finding an optimal schedule becomes NP-hard. CusADi2 addresses this with a windowed level schedule. It partitions a sequential schedule into consecutive windows of size $K$, applying level scheduling within each window and executing them in order. Setting $K \leq N$ guarantees hardware saturation constraints are met. At compile time, candidate sizes $K \in \{|\mathcal{W}|, |\mathcal{W}|/2, |\mathcal{W}|/4, \ldots\}$ are evaluated offline to automatically find the largest valid $K$.

### IV-C Hardware-Aware GPU Optimizations
Two additional techniques ensure peak execution efficiency on physical GPU hardware:

- **Staging**: Trajectory computations like MPC repeat the same function across $H$ timesteps. CusADi2 detects this repetitive structure, generates a schedule for a single step, and reuses it across all stages, significantly reducing schedule generation overhead.
- **Vertex Ordering**: NVIDIA GPUs execute identical instructions in lockstep across 32 threads (one warp). If different operations (e.g., $\sin$ and $\cos$) share the same level, warp divergence occurs, doubling execution steps. By sorting independent vertices within each level by operation type before assigning them to warps, warp divergence is minimized to maximize execution speed.

sections.heading: Benchmarking All 67 Robots: Dramatic Latency Reductions at Intermediate Batches
sections.summary: Comprehensive benchmarks across all 67 robots in the MuJoCo Menagerie show CusADi2 outperforming all existing GPU implementations by several to dozens of times, particularly at batch sizes of 64 to 4096 commonly used in online control.
sections.details:
To evaluate the method, 201 functions across forward kinematics, Jacobians, and Hessians (with up to 429,773 operations) were extracted from all 67 robots in the MuJoCo Menagerie (arms, hands, quadrupeds, humanoids, etc.). CusADi2 was compared against four GPU baselines (MuJoCo XLA, MuJoCo Warp, CusADi, and frax) and two CPU baselines using CasADi C-code generation (compute-only and including GPU-CPU transfer).

### V-A Latency Comparison with Baselines
Results clearly split across batch sizes $B$ (Fig. F1 A):
- **Intermediate Batch Regime ($64 \leq B \leq 4096$)**: This is the most critical range for online control. Here, intra-batch parallelization proves extremely powerful, achieving median speedups over CusADi of up to ~40x for forward kinematics, ~60x for Jacobians, and ~95x for Hessians. It remains several times faster than MuJoCo XLA and Warp. CusADi2 is the only GPU baseline to surpass the idealized CPU baseline as early as batch size 64.
- **Large Batch Regime ($B = 16384$)**: As GPU capacity saturates across batch instances alone, the performance gap narrows. Still, CusADi2 remains roughly 2x faster than MuJoCo XLA and Warp, maintaining a distinct edge on derivative calculations.
- **Small Batch Regime ($B < 16$)**: Due to higher single-core CPU clock speeds, the CPU is faster in isolated computation. However, when accounting for memory transfer overhead in an end-to-end GPU pipeline, CusADi2 matches or beats the CPU even at batch sizes of 1 to 16.

### V-B Which Robots Benefit Most?
On representative platforms like UR5e, Franka FR3, Unitree Go2, and Unitree G1, CusADi2 evaluates batch size 256 in under 40 microseconds. Interestingly, degrees of freedom (DOF) do not strictly correlate with latency. For example, the 92-DOF IIT SoftFoot computes more than twice as fast as the 85-DOF MS Human 700.

Analyzing the relationship between DAG shape and speedup (Fig. F1 B) reveals that speedup strongly correlates with the DAG's average width (parallelism). Robots with branching kinematic trees—such as quadrupeds, humanoids, and multi-fingered hands—benefit most from level parallelization and achieve dramatic speedups.

captions.F1: Speedup across all robots as a function of batch size (A) and the correlation between speedup and DAG average width / depth (B). CusADi2 outperforms existing methods at batch sizes 64 to 4096, showing that robots with wider computational graphs (higher parallelism) achieve the most dramatic speedups.

sections.heading: Downstream Application: Real-Time Execution of Safety-Filtered MPC
sections.summary: A sampling-based MPC with high-order control barrier functions (HOCBF) was evaluated on a Franka arm obstacle-avoidance task. CusADi2's low latency translated directly to complex second-order derivative safety evaluations, enabling high control rates.
sections.details:
The authors validated whether low latency in isolated benchmarks translates to end-to-end performance in practical robot control tasks.

### Task and Controller Setup
The task requires a Franka Panda arm to track waypoints while avoiding singularities, joint limits, self-collisions, and collisions with the floor and spherical obstacles. Control is handled by the predictive sampling planner in MuJoCo MPC, augmented with a high-order control barrier function (HOCBF) safety filter applied to candidate trajectories. Because HOCBF constraints require second-order forward kinematics derivatives (Hessians), MuJoCo Warp was excluded from this comparison due to its lack of Hessian support.

### Experimental Results
The controller executed 3 planner iterations per control step, evaluating $B$ rollout samples over a 0.7-second horizon (7 spline control points). In end-to-end latency measurements matching function-level tests, CusADi2 achieved lower latency than all other GPU backends across every tested batch size. This makes real-time, safety-constrained sampling-based MPC at 50 Hz a practical reality.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Directions
sections.summary: CusADi2 delivers the low GPU latency demanded by online control through intra-instance graph parallelization. While it currently assumes uniform operation runtimes, future work will integrate non-uniform operation costs and advanced techniques like warp specialization.
sections.details:
This paper presented CusADi2, a GPU library that parallelizes internal computational graphs within each instance alongside batch-level parallelization for robot dynamics and derivative computations. Benchmarks on all 67 robots in the MuJoCo Menagerie showed that CusADi2 outperforms existing GPU libraries and surpasses idealized CPU baselines at batch sizes of 64 to 4096, the sweet spot for online trajectory optimization. Robots with highly branched kinematic structures see the greatest performance gains.

The current scheduling model assumes every operation completes in a single uniform time unit, whereas real hardware exhibits varying latencies across operations. Future work will aim to further reduce latency by incorporating operation-specific execution costs into scheduling and leveraging advanced hardware techniques such as warp specialization.

takeaways: In GPU simulation and optimization, parallelizing intra-instance computational graphs—not just the batch dimension—is decisive for achieving low latency.
Because forward kinematics and Jacobian graphs for typical robots rarely saturate modern GPU core counts, level scheduling provides an effective, optimal solution.
Robots with branching kinematics (such as multi-fingered hands, quadrupeds, and humanoids) feature higher internal parallelism and gain the greatest speedups from CusADi2.
When the broader control pipeline resides on the GPU, staying on the GPU with CusADi2 can outperform the CPU even at tiny batch sizes (1 to 16) by eliminating data transfer overhead.
limitations: Scheduling assumes all primitive operations (e.g., additions and trigonometric functions) take one unit of time, ignoring variations in actual hardware execution latencies across operation types.
Finding optimal schedules in the saturated hardware regime is NP-hard, leaving the system reliant on windowing heuristics that yield suboptimal schedules.
Robots with long serial chains and minimal branching (such as simple single-arm manipulators) yield narrow computational graphs, limiting the speedup benefits of intra-instance parallelization.
